title: Teams Must Find a Way to Discuss the Undiscussables
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This Admired Leadership Field Note argues that even high-performing teams carry shared but unspoken beliefs, such as a strategy no one believes in, a leader no one trusts or a failing project. People stay silent because they fear defensiveness, being labelled negative or disloyal, and unpredictable aftershocks, and the silence compounds as each quiet person makes the next one's silence easier. The first burden falls on the leader, who must show openness by naming a hard truth about their own decisions, asking what is undiscussable and treating whoever speaks up as a hero. Team members can help by framing the issue as shared, avoiding accusations and presuming no motives, and opening with a line such as admitting they too have been avoiding it. Anonymous surveys or facilitated sessions can start the conversation when risk is high. The note closes by insisting that discussion needs a named owner and a check-back date, and that healthy teams are those that refuse to let an issue stay undiscussable for long.
points: Undiscussables persist because people expect the leader to react defensively, so how the leader responds to the first attempt decides whether anyone speaks again.
Leaders should demonstrate openness by naming a hard truth about their own decisions and asking directly what the team cannot say.
Raising an issue works better framed as a shared problem, without accusations or presumed motives, and a line like "I have been avoiding it too" opens doors a direct charge would close.
Anonymous surveys or facilitated sessions are workable on-ramps when the perceived risk is too high.
Discussion alone feeds cynicism, so every conversation needs a concrete next step with an owner and a check-back date.
quotes: Situations like a strategy no one believes in, a leader no one trusts, a project everyone knows is failing, or a toxic team member no one confronts are not unusual, even on high-performing teams.
An issue often becomes undiscussable when the team believes the leader is blind to the problem and will act defensively if it is raised.
Each time someone remains quiet, the next person finds it easier to do the same, and the issue grows harder to raise the longer it goes unspoken.

Claiming every topic is open for discussion is not enough. Leaders must show it by naming a hard truth about their own decisions, asking directly what is undiscussable, and treating the person with the courage to raise the issue as a hero, not a villain.
Framing the issue as a problem the whole team shares, avoiding accusations aimed at a single team member or the leader, and refusing to presume motives all encourage more open discussion.
A line as simple as “I think we have been avoiding talking about something, and I have been avoiding it too” often opens a conversation in a supportive way, where a direct charge would close it.

It’s not enough to openly discuss the issue. Discussion alone feeds the belief that nothing will change. The team needs a concrete step, with a named owner and a date to check back, so the discussion produces something.
The healthiest teams are not the ones without undiscussables. They are the teams that refuse to let an issue stay undiscussable for too long.
